new_statements.quote: 4.2113 Prosodeme. Drei prosodemische Einheiten, die [...] Merkmale Schalldruck, Tonhöhe und Vokallänge gekennzeichnet sind, können im KPS unterschieden werden [...] Das Vorkommen dieser drei Prosodeme ist an die vorletzte Silbe des Wortes gebunden. Distinktive Prosodeme konnten nicht festgestellt werden. Das ordinative Prosodem besitzt die Merkmale Druckakzent (d. h. [ver]stärkter Schalldruck), leichte Längung des silbentragenden Elementes der vorletzten Silbe des Wortes [...] - nicht immer - gehobenen Ton. Da das ordinative Prosodem in jeder Worteinheit vorkommt, bildet es [... die] Definition des Wortes im KPS.73 [Fn. 73:] Bei einigen Wörtern kommt das ordinative Prosodem auf der drittletzten oder letzten Silbe des Wortes [...]
new_statements.translation: 4.2113 Prosodemes. Three prosodemic units, characterised by the features loudness, pitch and vowel length, can be distinguished in KPS [Kenya Pidgin Swahili] ... The occurrence of these three prosodemes is bound to the penultimate syllable of the word. Distinctive [i.e. lexically contrastive] prosodemes could not be established. The ordinative prosodeme has the features stress accent (i.e. increased loudness), slight lengthening of the syllabic nucleus of the penultimate syllable of the word [and a] - not always - raised tone. Since the ordinative prosodeme occurs in every word unit, it forms [the basis for the] definition of the word in KPS. [fn. 73:] In some words the ordinative prosodeme falls on the antepenultimate or the final syllable of the word ...
new_statements.citation: Heine, Bernd. 1973. Pidgin-Sprachen im Bantu-Bereich (Kölner Beiträge zur Afrikanistik 3). Berlin: Dietrich Reimer.

new_statements.rule_in_words: In Kenya Pidgin Swahili (the up-country/Nairobi pidgin of which 'Kihindi', the Swahili used between Indians and Africans, is a named sub-dialect) word prosody is non-contrastive and fixed: every word carries an 'ordinative prosodeme' = stress (loudness + slight lengthening + usually raised pitch) on the penultimate syllable; question and emphasis prosodemes dock on the same syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing recoverable for KPS from the snippets (a snippet mentioning 'sekundären Akzent auf der vorletzten Silbe' appears to belong to another section, probably Fanagalo/comparative ch. 5).
new_statements.exceptions: Footnote 73: in some words the ordinative prosodeme falls on the antepenultimate or final syllable (the examples are cut off in the snippet).
new_statements.domain_note: Word domain ('Worteinheit'); Heine uses the obligatory penult prosodeme as the criterion for wordhood in KPS. CAUTION: this is Heine's KPS (Nairobi, mainly African L2 speakers), not a description of Cutchi-Swahili/Asian Swahili as such; read only through search snippets, no page image seen.
new_statements.identity_note: cutc1238 conflates two things named in Neale 1974: (a) 'Asian Swahili' / kiHindi / Kibabu (Maho G40A) = the second-language up-country Swahili of East African South Asians, and (b) 'Cutchi-Swahili' proper (Maho G40B) = a Kachchi-Swahili home mix of some Khoja Ismaili and Ithna-asheri families (Zanzibar, coastal towns). The only stress wording located (Heine 1973) is for Kenya Pidgin Swahili as a whole (Nairobi, mostly African speakers), which Heine says includes the 'Kihindi' sub-dialect; it is therefore an adjacent-variety statement, not a description of cutc1238 itself, and Glottolog would file Heine's KPS nearer the Settla/up-country pidgin entries than under cutc1238. If variety (b) is taken as the referent, its prosody would more likely follow Kachchi (kach1277) than Swahili; no source addresses this.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Neale 1974, p. 76 (last lines of the page; the passage ends at the p. 77 running header 'LANGUAGE IN KENYA'), inside section '1. PHONOLOGY': 'Homorganic nasals are lost in some forms and expanded with anaptyptic vowels (ə in unstressed position, u elsewhere) in others: mC > C e.g. mbili- bili, moC mchanga->machanga [p. 77] muC mtu mutu, amka->muka, nC>C e.g. mndani->dani, nC > neC e.g. Ngara>Nagara' (scanned prints the schwa as '9'). Recovered with item-restricted FTS probes '"unstressed position"', '"anaptyptic"', '"u elsewhere"', '"machanga"' (files). It presupposes word stress in Asian Swahili (anaptyctic vowel quality is conditioned by unstressed position) but states no stress placement…

sources.note: Nothing on stress. Wikipedia notes only segmental adaptation of Swahili loans to Kutchi (sahani > saani). Glottolog files cutc1238 under Sabaki > Swahili > Mombasa-area Swahili and lists Neale 1974 as the sole descriptive reference (Glottolog's fullest description is a grammar sketch).

sources.note: Names 'kiSwahili cha kiHindi', the trade Swahili of Indian shopkeepers (pp. 6, 25), as one of the up-country contact varieties characterised by morphological simplification, but gives no phonology for it. Its stress statement (§2.1.3.1 'Stress occurs as a rule on the penultimate vowel phoneme..') is for Standard Swahili, not for cutc1238.
